nature-es-001.title: The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment: a health check for the planet
nature-es-001.text: More than 1300 authors from 95 countries spent four years on one question: what are people doing to the ecosystems that keep them alive? Their answer was the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, a United Nations-backed study called for in 2000, launched in 2001 and published in 2005. An earlier book, {{ref:nature-es-004}}, was described as a catalyst for it. The assessment popularized the term ecosystem services, meaning the benefits people gain from ecosystems. It sorted them into four groups: provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting, with supporting services underpinning the other three. Its findings were sobering. In the past 50 years humans had changed ecosystems faster and more widely than ever before, mainly to meet demand for food, fresh water, timber, fiber and fuel. Those changes made many lives better and fueled development. They also degraded many ecosystem services and made some groups poorer. The bottom line was blunt. Human actions were depleting Earth's natural capital so much that ecosystems' ability to sustain future generations could no longer be taken for granted. The next UN report on the state of biodiversity did not come until the global assessment of {{ref:nature-gov-020}} in 2019.

nature-es-006.title: Putting a price on nature's work
nature-es-006.text: What is clean water worth to a fisher? The economics of ecosystem services tries to answer questions like that, expressing services in economic terms so their value can be weighed in decisions. It translates scientific knowledge into comparable units of impact on people's lives. People decide for many reasons, but overall trends reveal what a society prefers, and value can be inferred from them. There are six main ways to value services in money, from avoided cost and {{ref:nature-val-093}} to travel cost, hedonic pricing and {{ref:nature-val-085}}. One of them, factor income, counts how a service raises incomes, as when cleaner water increases the fish catch and fishers' earnings. Scale is a stubborn problem, because ecological data gathered at one place and time may not hold at another. Some reject the whole exercise. Salles (2011) argued that biodiversity's total value is infinite, since no one can live without it. As of 2012 many companies still did not grasp how much they depend on ecosystems.

nature-es-005.title: From Plato's springs to a scientific term
nature-es-005.text: Around 400 BC Plato understood that cutting down forests could cause soil erosion and dry up springs. The idea took a very long time to get a name. Modern thinking probably began in 1864, when Marsh challenged the belief that Earth's resources are unlimited by pointing to changing soil fertility around the Mediterranean. In the late 1940s Henry Fairfield Osborn Jr, William Vogt and {{ref:nature-hist-051}} argued that people depend on the environment. In 1956 Paul Sears stressed ecosystems' role in processing wastes and reusing nutrients. By 1970 the warnings were starker: Paul Ehrlich and Rosa Weigert said human activity could destroy the ecological systems our species depends on. That year a report spoke of 'environmental services', listing insects that carry pollen, fisheries, regulating climate and flood control. {{ref:nature-hist-060}} coined 'natural capital' in his 1973 book, {{ref:nature-hist-019}}. In the 1990s two works became seminal: Daily's {{ref:nature-es-004}} and Costanza and colleagues' first attempt to put a money value on ecosystem services. The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment then popularized the idea, and 'ecosystem services' became the standard term.

nature-es-009.title: Protecting services when a price tag is not enough
nature-es-009.text: Ecosystem services are estimated to add $125 trillion to $140 trillion to the economy each year. Even so, protecting them is hard. Decision-makers must balance present and future needs, often with valid but incomplete information. Existing laws are often seen as inadequate because they rest on human-health standards, which do not match what healthy ecosystems require. As of 2005, local to regional collective management was considered suitable for services such as pollinating crops and for resources like water. Since the 1990s, markets have grown that sell credits for protecting services, such as guarding carbon sinks or restoring service providers. These schemes need clearly defined rights to land, often missing in developing countries, and they raise worries about inconsistent compensation. Because protecting services often overlaps with protecting biodiversity, some suggest merging the two goals. Law lags behind. As of 2018 the concept was not properly built into international and regional law, though {{ref:nature-gov-030}} targets conserving, restoring and sustainably using ecosystem services. The stakes keep rising: climate-driven shifts in biomes may cut services by 9% globally by 2100.

nature-es-011.title: Tracing a product's footprint on nature's services
nature-es-011.text: Every product leaves a trail of environmental pressures, from the land cleared to make it to the nutrients that wash into rivers. {{ref:nature-acct-050}} tracks those pressures. Its impact methods now link them, such as land-use change and eutrophication, to changes in ecological functions and ecosystem services. A 2026 review found three main kinds of model: land-use impact models, extended ecosystem quality models and inventory-based models. They differ in the services, ecosystems and indicators they cover, and in whether they count supply, demand or both. That makes comparison hard. Freshwater and marine services remain poorly represented, so the field needs more consistent guidance.

nature-es-123.title: Nature's contributions to people: a broader name, or a new label?
nature-es-123.text: In 2017 the 5th plenary meeting of {{ref:nature-gov-020}} made a decision about words. Its assessments would now speak of nature's contributions to people: all the ways nature benefits people. The phrase replaced 'nature's benefits to people' from then on. The aim was to bring diverse worldviews, including indigenous and local knowledge, into biodiversity assessments. Not everyone was persuaded. Some scientists objected that the term was confusing and not significantly different from ecosystem services. Whether it adds anything beyond that older concept remains a genuine disagreement.

nature-es-002.title: Clean air, fresh water and the work behind them
nature-es-002.text: Clean air and plentiful fresh water are ecological goods. Purifying that air and water is a service, and so are breaking down wastes, pollinating crops, refilling underground water stores and mitigating greenhouse gases. Together they are the economic benefits of ecosystems' natural workings. Biodiversity underlies them all. {{ref:nature-hist-053}}'s original definition kept goods and services apart, but Costanza and colleagues and the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment lumped both together as ecosystem services. They are a kind of public good. They are also being lost at an unsustainable rate, especially where land is converted from its natural state and loses its ecological functions. One remedy is to create a market, in which society demands these goods and services and public and private landowners supply them. Paying farmers to set land aside marks a shift from 'polluter pays' to 'beneficiary pays'. Regulation, land-care programs, eco-labeling, offset credits and tax rebates can secure supply too.

nature-es-007.title: When one service gains and another pays
nature-es-007.text: Fertilizer spread on fields in the US Midwest grows abundant crops. Washed downriver, the same heavy fertilizer use has degraded fisheries in the Gulf of Mexico. This is an ecosystem service trade-off: using or boosting one service reduces others or harms some people. The opposite is a synergy, where services rise together. Nature's cycling of nutrients, it turns out, cannot simply be dialed to a best level. In some areas farm production competes with restoring ecosystems. Decisions also create winners and losers, as when water moves from poor to rich users or a protected wetland limits fishing rights. Yet the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment found many ways to enhance particular services while easing trade-offs or creating synergies. Valuation can give extra weight to a service that is irreplaceable, or to bundles of services that come together. Tools such as the Freshwater Health Index help managers weigh the options, and landscape planning tries to balance food production, conservation and livelihoods.

nature-es-010.title: Deciding what to do with the land
nature-es-010.text: Land-use decisions that touch ecosystem services are messy by nature. They mean weighing ecology, technology, society and the economy together. They are usually spatial, always have several objectives, and rest on uncertain data, models and estimates. Regulators, developers, residents and NGOs all have a say; usually the best science combined with stakeholder values drives the process. Researchers have modeled stakeholders as agents and used repeated random simulations to capture uncertainty in landowner choices. Others have blended uncertain science with stakeholder input in probability models. Images of land taken from above can track the health and extent of the vegetation and ground cover that provide services.

nature-es-008.title: Who gains from nature's services
nature-es-008.text: Some services land right on the doorstep. Fresh water, food and beauty directly shape the livelihoods of people who live near an ecosystem. Others arrive from a distance: regulating climate or holding back erosion affects people indirectly, far from the source. Beneficiaries are all the people who gain from a given service. Humans are not the only ones, since ecological goods and services benefit all living things, animals and plants included. In private payment deals, beneficiaries are expected to pay less than the welfare gain the service gives them. Paying landowners who supply services marks a shift from 'polluter pays' to 'beneficiary pays'.

nature-es-004.title: Nature's Services: the 1997 book that framed a field
nature-es-004.text: In 1997 {{ref:nature-hist-053}} edited a book with a plain, insistent title: Nature's Services: Societal Dependence on Natural Ecosystems. It opens with her introduction, 'What are Ecosystem Services', followed by a history of the idea by Harold Mooney and Paul Ehrlich. The book laid out the framework still widely used for understanding nature's benefits to people. With Costanza and colleagues' global valuation, it became one of the two seminal 1990s works on the subject. It served as a model for ecosystem regulation in several regions and was a catalyst for the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment.

openers.es: In 1997 Gretchen Daily's edited book Nature's Services laid out a framework for something people had long taken for granted: the economic benefits that flow from the natural workings of ecosystems. In 2005 a United Nations-backed study, the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, carried that idea around the world. This part follows ecosystem services from their roots to their hardest questions. What is nature's work worth, who gains from it, and what happens when boosting one service drains another? Along the way it meets nature's own recycling system, the cycles that keep matter moving back into new life.
openers.the-ecosystem-services-idea: The notion that ecosystems serve people began as ancient observation and became a standard scientific term. Gretchen Daily's 1997 book gave it a framework, and the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, launched in 2001, made it famous. This chapter asks what the idea means and who benefits, whether they live beside an ecosystem or feel its effects from far away. It follows economists trying to express services in money so they can be weighed in decisions. It also meets the hard parts: services that rise only at another's expense, land-use choices that juggle ecology and economics, and a newer name from IPBES, {{ref:nature-es-123}}.

reviews.the-ecosystem-services-idea: Plato's worry about vanishing springs grew, over many centuries, into a standard term carried by Gretchen Daily's 1997 book and the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment. That assessment found humans had changed ecosystems faster than ever, buying real gains at the cost of degraded services and deeper poverty for some. Economists answered by expressing services in money, from replacement costs to fishers' rising incomes, though some argue nature's total value is infinite. Every choice has winners and losers, as Midwest fertilizer feeding crops while degrading Gulf fisheries shows. Protecting services means weighing ecology and economics under uncertainty, with laws and markets that still lag behind.
